In Java multithreading, ConcurrentHashMap stands as the quintessential thread-safe alternative to synchronized maps like Hashtable or Collections.synchronizedMap. However, its internal architecture underwent a massive paradigm shift. Pre-Java 8 implementations relied heavily on Segment Locking—a structural partitioning technique where the map was divided into a fixed number of segments, each extending ReentrantLock. This allowed multiple threads to write concurrently to the map as long as their target keys hashed into different segments. While a significant improvement over global synchronization, this design suffered from fixed sizing, high memory overhead, and lock contention if the concurrency level was misconfigured at initialization.

Java 8 completely redesigned ConcurrentHashMap, discarding segment locking in favor of a hybrid approach utilizing Compare-And-Swap (CAS) operations combined with synchronized blocks. Instead of locking entire segments, Java 8 approaches synchronization at the granularity of individual hash bins (bucket nodes). CAS is leveraged for lock-free insertion of the first node in an empty bin, while synchronized blocks are applied strictly to the head node of a populated bucket during collision handling, treeification, or resizing. This dramatically reduces lock contention, lowers memory consumption by removing Segment objects, and dramatically improves throughput under heavy concurrent read/write workloads.

rows: Bin-level (synchronized on individual bucket head node)

Low (nodes directly inside the main array)
Singly-linked lists that dynamically treeify into TreeBins

items: In Java 8+, when multiple threads attempt to insert into an uninitialized bucket, the first thread uses a CAS operation (via VarHandle or Unsafe) to atomically place the node. If the CAS fails due to a race, the thread yields or assists via table initialization checks.

When a hash collision occurs on a populated bucket, Java 8 acquires a monitor lock strictly on the bin's head node using a synchronized block. This ensures that threads accessing other buckets remain entirely unblocked.

If a single bin grows beyond TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (default 8) and the overall array capacity exceeds MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY (default 64), the linear linked list transforms into a balanced Red-Black Tree (TreeBin), bounding worst-case lookup time from O(N) down to O(log N).

parsed_answer.content: A classic production trap with ConcurrentHashMap is assuming that compound operations like check-then-act (e.g., if(map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)) are atomic. Even though individual methods like get() and put() are thread-safe, composite sequences require atomic methods like putIfAbsent(), compute(), or merge() to prevent race conditions. Additionally, be aware that size() and mappingCount() in Java 8+ return estimations rather than exact counts during concurrent structural modifications.

title: ConcurrentHashMap — segment locking (pre-Java 8) vs CAS + synchronized (Java 8+)
